claims.claim: The Farmer Giles chronicle fixes its events by the church calendar (St Nicholas' Day, Christmas Eve, 14 January) inside a legendary span 'between Brutus and King Arthur'.

Farmer Giles's pose as a translated manuscript with commentary on its origins and dubious place-name etymology parodies scholarly works including the Prologue to Tolkien's own Lord of the Rings, mocking the medieval appeal to authority.
claims.quote: parody of scholarly works, including the prologue

claims.claim: The tale's narrator was 'Daddy' in the oral original, became 'the family jester', and took on a formal scholarly tone when the story was enlarged by half for an academic essay club in 1938.
claims.source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)

claims.claim: By its 1949 publication the children's tale had acquired the mock-scholarly foreword, so the record register was a deliberate late addition rather than the story's native voice.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell, 'Farmer Giles of Ham: Comedy in Faërie?' (DBU)

claims.claim: Shippey identifies the Middle Kingdom of Farmer Giles with early Mercia, its capital possibly Tamworth, so the record's geography is a calque on real English history.
Kullmann finds the Prologue imitates the non-fictional prose of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnography, while the Note on the Shire Records mimics works of historiography.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, pp. 46–47)
claims.quote: non-fictional prose of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century ethnography

claims.claim: 'Concerning Hobbits' places the text in the stylistic mode of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism, like a treatise on regional folklore, signalling to the reader a departure from modern novelistic conventions.
claims.quote: a certain strain of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism

claims.claim: Halbrooks argues Tolkien's greatest strength is that he very carefully adjusts his prose style and even his generic conventions according to the narrative circumstances.
claims.quote: he very carefully adjusts his prose style

claims.claim: The Shire is 'calqued' on England element by element: three founding tribes, a forgotten origin, founding brothers with horse-names, and a 272-year peace between battles matching the 270 years since Sedgemoor.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'

claims.claim: Organisationally the Shire, with its mayors, musters, moots and Shirriffs, is an old-fashioned and idealised England.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'

claims.claim: Modern names are perceived as labels isomorphic with reality, so a dense name-stock weighs fantasy down with repeated implicit assurances that the things labelled exist; this is strongest in the Shire's map, account and history.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: repeated implicit assurances of the existence of the things

claims.claim: Speakers in The Lord of the Rings have a strong tendency to talk like historical maps, reeling off names and river courses, a habit shared by Aragorn, Celeborn, Gimli, Gandalf and Meriadoc.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: talk like maps, historical ones at that

claims.claim: The Prologue says 'pipe-weed' rather than tobacco because the imported word would sound wrong, and hedges its botany with a Latin binomial instead.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth

claims.claim: The Note on the Shire Records credits Meriadoc with a Herblore of the Shire, a Reckoning of Years comparing calendars, and a treatise on Old Words and Names, so the record cites fictional reference works by title.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), quoting the Note
claims.quote: Old Words and Names in the Shire

claims.claim: 'Concerning Pipe-weed' began as a lengthy speech by Merry in a draft of 'The Road to Isengard' that was removed and reworked into the Prologue, so dialogue was converted into record.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Prologue (The Lord of the Rings)'
claims.quote: a lengthy speech of Merry about pipe-weed
